claim: The natverse is a suite of interoperable open-source R packages for neuroanatomical data analysis.
source: To facilitate this, we have developed a suite of interoperable open-source R packages called the natverse.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract of the manuscript.

claim: The natverse allows users to read local and remote data.
source: The natverse allows users to read local and remote data, perform popular analyses including visualisation and clustering and graph-theoretic analysis of neuronal branching.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a capability of the natverse.

claim: The natverse enables comparison across many neurons of morphology and connectivity after imaging or co-registration within a common template space.
source: Unlike most tools, the natverse enables comparison across many neurons of morphology and connectivity after imaging or co-registration within a common template space.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a distinctive feature of the natverse.

claim: The natverse enables transformations between different template spaces and imaging modalities.
source: The natverse also enables transformations between different template spaces and imaging modalities.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a capability of the natverse.

claim: The natverse integrates the vast majority of Drosophila neuroanatomical light microscopy and electron microscopy connectomic datasets.
source: We demonstrate tools that integrate the vast majority of Drosophila neuroanatomical light microscopy and electron microscopy connectomic datasets.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a demonstrated capability.

claim: Neuroanatomy has become a large-scale, digital and quantitative discipline.
source: Neuroanatomy has become a large-scale, digital and quantitative discipline.
evidence: Stated in the introduction as context for the work.

claim: Improvements in sample preparation and imaging increasingly enable the collection of large 3D image volumes containing complete neuronal morphologies in the context of whole brains or brain regions.
source: Improvements in sample preparation and imaging increasingly enable the collection of large 3D image volumes containing complete neuronal morphologies in the context of whole brains or brain regions.
evidence: Stated in the introduction as background information.

claim: ImageJ/Fiji is a flexible but open source platform for image analysis.
source: This has been amply demonstrated by flexible but open source platforms such as ImageJ/Fiji for image analysis (Schindelin et al., 2012) or Bioconductor for bioinformatics (Huber et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited as an example of successful open source platforms.

claim: Bioconductor is a flexible but open source platform for bioinformatics.
source: This has been amply demonstrated by flexible but open source platforms such as ImageJ/Fiji for image analysis (Schindelin et al., 2012) or Bioconductor for bioinformatics (Huber et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited as an example of successful open source platforms.

claim: Free and open-source tools aid collaboration and reproducibility, and reduce the overhead when switching between different types of analysis.
source: One important consequence of these free and open-source tools is that they aid collaboration and reproducibility, and reduce the overhead when switching between different types of analysis.
evidence: Stated as a motivation for creating the natverse.

claim: A number of software tools are already available to analyse neuronal data.
source: A number of software tools are already available to analyse neuronal data (Billeci et al., 2013; Brown et al., 2005; Cuntz et al., 2010; Feng et al., 2015; Gensel et al., 2010; Glaser and Glaser, 1990; Ho et al., 2011; Katz and Plaza, 2019; Kim et al., 2015; Meijering et al., 2004; Myatt et al., 2012; Narro et al., 2007; Peng et al., 2014; Pool et al., 2008; Saalfeld et al., 2009; Schmitz et al., 2011; Wearne et al., 2005).
evidence: Cited as existing work in the field.

claim: Most existing neuronal analysis tools focus on image processing and the morphological analysis options available are fairly basic.
source: However, most focus on image processing and the morphological analysis options available are fairly basic, such as examining arbour lengths or performing Sholl analyses (Sholl, 1953).
evidence: Stated as a limitation of existing tools.

claim: The trees toolbox has particularly strong support for morphological analysis of neurons but focuses on individual neurons in isolation rather than neurons within the volume of the brain as a whole.
source: Of these, the trees toolbox (Cuntz et al., 2010), has particularly strong support for morphological analysis of neurons but focuses on individual neurons in isolation rather than neurons within the volume of the brain as a whole.
evidence: Cited as a limitation of an existing tool.

claim: Recent technological advances have made acquiring large amounts of neuronal morphology data in their whole-brain contexts feasible across phyla.
source: Recent technological advances have made acquiring large amounts of neuronal morphology data in their whole-brain contexts feasible across phyla (Chiang et al., 2011; Cook et al., 2019; Economo et al., 2016; Jenett et al., 2012; Kunst et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019; Oh et al., 2014; Ohyama et al., 2015; Ryan et al., 2016; Winnubst et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited as recent progress in the field.

claim: Image data are typically registered against a template space, allowing one to compare data from many brains directly and quantitatively.
source: Image data are typically registered against a template space, allowing one to compare data from many brains directly and quantitatively.
evidence: Stated as a common practice in the field.

claim: Template space registration significantly aids the classification of neuronal cell types because it allows type classification relative to the arbours of other neuronal types and anatomical subvolumes.
source: This significantly aids the classification of neuronal cell types because it allows type classification relative to the arbours of other neuronal types (Sümbül et al., 2014) and anatomical subvolumes.
evidence: Stated as a benefit of template space registration with citation.

claim: Template spaces are often different across studies or laboratories, hindering data integration.
source: However, while this enables the comparison of data within a given study, template spaces are often different across studies or laboratories, hindering data integration.
evidence: Stated as a problem in the field.

claim: A distinctive feature of the natverse, as compared with other available tools, is to analyse neurons within and across template spaces and to simplify access to a wide range of data sources.
source: A distinctive feature of the natverse, as compared with other available tools, is to analyse neurons within and across template spaces and to simplify access to a wide range of data sources.
evidence: Stated as a key distinguishing feature of the natverse.

claim: Neurons can be read from local files or from online repositories and web-based reconstruction environments.
source: Neurons can be read from local files or from online repositories (Ascoli et al., 2007; Chiang et al., 2011; Economo et al., 2016; Jenett et al., 2012; Kunst et al., 2019; Winnubst et al., 2019) and web-based reconstruction environments (Katz and Plaza, 2019; Saalfeld et al., 2009; Schneider-Mizell et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated as a capability of the natverse with citations.

claim: The natverse can be installed in two lines of code as described on the project website (https://natverse.org).
source: The natverse can be installed in two lines of code as described on the project website (https://natverse.org).
evidence: Stated as a feature of the natverse installation process.

claim: Every function in the natverse is documented with a large number of examples based on bundled or publicly available data.
source: Every function is documented with a large number of examples based on bundled or publicly available data.
evidence: Stated as a feature of the natverse documentation.

claim: Example pipeline code, and code to generate the figures in this manuscript is available through https://github.com/natverse/nat.examples.
source: Example pipeline code, and code to generate the figures in this manuscript is available through https://github.com/natverse/nat.examples.
evidence: Stated as a resource provided by the authors.

claim: Online community support is provided through the nat-user mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/nat-user.
source: We provide online community support through our nat-user mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/nat-user.
evidence: Stated as a support resource for users.

claim: The natverse has recently been employed for large-scale analysis of zebrafish data.
source: The natverse has recently been employed for large-scale analysis of zebrafish data (Kunst et al., 2019), and we provide examples across a range of invertebrate and vertebrate species.
evidence: Cited as a recent application of the natverse.

claim: Using the natverse, bridging registrations have been created that transform data from one template to another along with mirroring registrations.
source: Using the natverse, we have created bridging registrations that transform data from one template to another along with mirroring registrations (e.g. left-to-right hemisphere) and made these easily deployable.
evidence: Stated as work done using the natverse.

claim: The natverse unifies all publicly available Drosophila neuroanatomical datasets, including those image data for genetic resources and whole brain connectomics.
source: This unifies all publicly available Drosophila neuroanatomical datasets, including those image data for genetic resources and whole brain connectomics.
evidence: Stated as an achievement of the natverse.

claim: R is a leading platform for bioinformatics and general data analysis.
source: We have opted to develop our software in R, a leading platform for bioinformatics and general data analysis.
evidence: Stated as a reason for choosing R.

claim: R is free and open source, and is supported by high-quality integrated development environments (e.g. Rstudio).
source: R is free and open source, and is supported by high-quality integrated development environments (e.g. Rstudio).
evidence: Stated as advantages of R.

claim: R features a well-defined system for creating and distributing extension packages that bundle code and documentation.
source: It features a well-defined system for creating and distributing extension packages that bundle code and documentation.
evidence: Stated as a feature of R.

claim: R packages can easily be installed from high-quality curated repositories (CRAN, Bioconductor) as well as via GitHub.
source: These can easily be installed from high-quality curated repositories (CRAN, Bioconductor) as well as via GitHub.
evidence: Stated as a feature of R package distribution.

claim: R supports a range of reproducible research strategies including reports and notebooks and integrates with the leading cross-platform tools in this area (jupyter, binder).
source: R supports a range of reproducible research strategies including reports and notebooks and integrates with the leading cross-platform tools in this area (jupyter, binder).
evidence: Stated as a feature of R.

claim: The core package of the natverse is the Neuroanatomy Toolbox, nat.
source: The core package of the natverse is the Neuroanatomy Toolbox, nat.
evidence: Stated as the central package of the natverse.

claim: nat supports 3D visualisation and analysis of neuroanatomical data, especially tracings of single neurons.
source: It supports 3D visualisation and analysis of neuroanatomical data (Figure 1a), especially tracings of single neurons (Figure 1b).
evidence: Stated as a capability of nat with reference to figures.

claim: nat allows a user to read neuronal data from a variety of popular data formats produced by neuron reconstruction tools.
source: nat allows a user to read neuronal data from a variety of popular data formats produced by neuron reconstruction tools (Figure 1a).
evidence: Stated as a capability of nat with reference to a figure.

claim: nat can read a collection of SWC files with a single command.
source: Typical image analysis pipelines include imaging neurons with confocal microscopy, reconstructing them using Fiji Simple Neurite Tracer (Longair et al., 2011) then saving them as SWC files (Cannon et al., 1998); nat can read a collection of such files with a single command.
evidence: Stated as a capability of nat with citations.

claim: The natverse is developed using modern software best practices including revision control, code review, unit testing, continuous integration, and comprehensive code coverage.
source: The natverse is developed using modern software best practices including revision control, code review, unit testing, continuous integration, and comprehensive code coverage.
evidence: Stated as a development practice for the natverse.

claim: Developing sets of functions in separate packages helps compartmentalise development, ease troubleshooting and divides the natverse into documented units that users can search to find the more specific code examples or functions that they need.
source: Developing sets of functions in separate packages helps compartmentalise development, ease troubleshooting and divides the natverse into documented units that users can search to find the more specific code examples or functions that they need.
evidence: Stated as a benefit of the package structure.

claim: A single wrapper package, natverse, is provided that results in the installation of all packages and their dependencies when installed.
source: We therefore provide a single wrapper package, natverse; installing this results in the installation of all packages and their dependencies, immediately giving the user all the capabilities described in this paper (Figure 1a).
evidence: Stated as a feature of the natverse installation with reference to a figure.

claim: Natverse packages have already been used in recent publications from the authors' lab.
source: Natverse packages have already been used in recent publications from our lab (Cachero et al., 2010; Costa et al., 2016; Dolan et al., 2019; Dolan et al., 2018a; Dolan et al., 2018b; Frechter et al., 2019; Grosjean et al., 2011; Huoviala et al., 2018; Jefferis et al., 2007) and others (Clemens et al., 2018; Clemens et al., 2015; Eichler et al., 2017; Felsenberg et al., 2018; Jeanne et al., 2018; Kunst et al., 2019; Saumweber et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2018), with the nat.nblast packaged described in Costa et al., 2016.
evidence: Cited as evidence of prior use of the natverse.

claim: Confirmed stable versions of nat, nat.templatebrains, nat.nblast, nat.utils and nabor can be downloaded from the centralised R package repository, CRAN.
source: Confirmed stable versions of nat, nat.templatebrains, nat.nblast, nat.utils and nabor can be downloaded from the centralised R package repository, CRAN, with developmental versions available from our GitHub page (https://github.com/natverse/).
evidence: Stated as a distribution method for stable versions.

claim: Developmental versions of natverse packages are available from the authors' GitHub page (https://github.com/natverse/).
source: Confirmed stable versions of nat, nat.templatebrains, nat.nblast, nat.utils and nabor can be downloaded from the centralised R package repository, CRAN, with developmental versions available from our GitHub page (https://github.com/natverse/).
evidence: Stated as a distribution method for developmental versions.

claim: Natverse packages can be thought of as belonging to four main groups.
source: In brief, natverse packages can be thought of as belonging to four main groups (Figure 1a).
evidence: Stated as an organizational structure with reference to a figure.

claim: The natverse provides functions for morphological and graph-theoretic analyses of neurons, collections of neurons, neurons as vector clouds and neurons as tree graphs.
source: The natverse provides functions for morphological and graph-theoretic analyses of neurons, collections of neurons, neurons as vector clouds and neurons as tree graphs (Figure 2a).
evidence: Stated as a capability with reference to a figure.

claim: The natverse mainly operates with skeleton data.
source: The natverse mainly operates with skeleton data, but the geometry of neuron mesh data can be analysed using the more general R packages Rvcg and Morpho (Schlager, 2017).
evidence: Stated as the primary data type with citation for mesh data analysis.

claim: The natverse represents skeletonised neurons as neuron objects, with the neuron's geometry in the standard SWC format.
source: The natverse represents skeletonised neurons as neuron objects, with the neuron's geometry in the standard SWC format where each node in the skeleton has its own integer identifier.
evidence: Stated as the data representation used.

claim: Objects of class neuron are lists of data objects describing properties such as the 3D position and interconnectivity of points in a neuron.
source: Objects of class neuron are lists of data objects, like data.frames, describing properties such as the 3D position and interconnectivity of points in a neuron.
evidence: Stated as a description of the neuron object class.

claim: Objects of class neuronlist are lists of neuron objects, representing one or more neurons, with some attached metadata.
source: Objects of class neuronlist are lists of neuron objects, representing one or more neurons, with some attached metadata.
evidence: Stated as a description of the neuronlist object class.

claim: A useful function with methods for neuron objects and neuronlist objects is summary.
source: A useful function with methods for neuron objects and neuronlist objects is summary.
evidence: Stated as a useful function.

claim: The summary function gives the user counts for tree nodes, branch points, leaf nodes and the total combined cable length of a neuron.
source: This gives the user counts for tree nodes, branch points, leaf nodes and the total combined cable length of a neuron (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Stated as the output of the summary function with reference to a figure.

claim: The natverse helps users to analyse neuronal skeletons with respect to volume objects that might represent neuroanatomical structures on a scale from whole neural tissues to neuropil subvolumes.
source: The natverse also helps users to analyse neuronal skeletons with respect to volume objects that might represent neuroanatomical structures on a scale from whole neural tissues to neuropil subvolumes.
evidence: Stated as a capability of the natverse.

claim: 3D objects from diverse sources can be visualised and analysed with nat, and their volumes can be calculated.
source: 3D objects from diverse sources can be visualised and analysed with nat, and we can calculate their volumes (Figure 3a).
evidence: Stated as a capability with reference to a figure.

claim: The nat function make_model allows a user to interactively create their own 3D objects from 3D points.
source: By using the nat function make_model, a user can interactively create their own 3D objects from, for example, 3D points from a neuron's cable or its synapses (Figure 3b); points can easily be retrieved by giving the function a labelled data.frame, matrix, neuron, neuronlist, hxsurf or mesh3d object (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated as a capability with reference to figures.

claim: Using the nat function prune_in_volume, a skeleton can be cut to include or exclude the cable within a given volume.
source: Using the nat function prune_in_volume, a skeleton can be cut to include or exclude the cable within a given volume, while the function pointsinside can tell a user which synapses lie within a standard neuropil segmentation (Figure 3c).
evidence: Stated as a capability with reference to a figure.

claim: The function pointsinside can tell a user which synapses lie within a standard neuropil segmentation.
source: Using the nat function prune_in_volume, a skeleton can be cut to include or exclude the cable within a given volume, while the function pointsinside can tell a user which synapses lie within a standard neuropil segmentation (Figure 3c).
evidence: Stated as a capability with reference to a figure.

claim: The natverse is a flexible platform that allows users to easily write their own R code to support intricate procedures.
source: Because the natverse is a flexible platform that allows users to easily write their own R code to support intricate procedures, very specific analyses can be performed.
evidence: Stated as a feature of the natverse.

claim: The natverse contains functions to infer connectivity from light-level data, including potential_synapses and overlap.
source: The natverse contains other functions to infer connectivity from light-level data, including potential_synapses, an implementation of a synapse prediction algorithm that makes use of spatial proximity and approach angle (Stepanyants and Chklovskii, 2005), and overlap, a simpler algorithm that measures the putative overlap in Euclidean space between neuron pairs (Frechter et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated as capabilities with citations.

claim: Neuronal cell type is a useful classification in neuroscience.
source: Neuronal cell type is a useful classification in neuroscience (Bates et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated with citation.

claim: Neuronal cell typing can be done by expert examination, purely by morphological clustering, or a combination of both.
source: Neuronal cell typing can be done by expert examination (Helmstaedter et al., 2013), purely by morphological clustering (Jeanne and Wilson, 2015), or a combination of both (Frechter et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated with citations.

claim: Many neurogeometric algorithms for assessing similarity exist.
source: Many neurogeometric algorithms for assessing similarity exist.
evidence: Stated as background information.

claim: Algorithms that are dependent on neurons' relative positioning in a template space have typically met with greater success than those that are invariant to the 3D embedding space.
source: Some are invariant to the 3D embedding space (Li et al., 2017; Sholl, 1953; Wan et al., 2015), but those that are dependent on neurons' relative positioning in a template space have typically met with greater success (Li et al., 2017; Zhao and Plaza, 2014).
evidence: Stated with citations.

claim: NBLAST is a recent morphological similarity algorithm.
source: NBLAST (Costa et al., 2016) is a recent morphological similarity algorithm (Frechter et al., 2019; Jeanne et al., 2018; Kohl et al., 2013; Kunst et al., 2019; Masse et al., 2012; Strutz et al., 2014; Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated with citations.

claim: NBLAST is included in the natverse in the nat.nblast package.
source: NBLAST is included in the natverse in our nat.nblast package (Costa et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated with citation.

claim: In many parts of mammalian nervous systems, morphologically similar neurons are repeated in space, and so aligning neurons to one another, without a specified template space, is sufficient for quantitative comparison.
source: In many parts of mammalian nervous systems, morphologically similar neurons are repeated in space, and so aligning neurons to one another, without a specified template space, is sufficient for quantitative comparison (Figure 4a).
evidence: Stated with reference to a figure.

claim: NBLAST scores can be hierarchically clustered in R, plotted as a dendrogram, and used to visualize morphological groups at a defined group number or cut height.
source: NBLAST scores can be hierarchically clustered in R, plotted as a dendrogram, and used to visualize morphological groups at a defined group number or cut height (Figure 4a).
evidence: Stated as a capability with reference to a figure.

claim: Morphological clustering forms a good starting point for cell typing, but might not be in exact agreement with manually defined cell types.
source: Often, this forms a good starting point for cell typing, but might not be in exact agreement with manually defined cell types (Figure 4b).
evidence: Stated as an observation with reference to a figure.

claim: Disagreement between morphological clustering and manual cell typing can be due to neuron reconstructions being differently severed by the field of view or size of the tissue sample collected.
source: This can be due to neuron reconstructions being differently severed by the field of view or size of the tissue sample collected (Helmstaedter et al., 2013), or due to registration offsets between registered neuronal skeletons (Chiang et al., 2011; Kunst et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated as a reason with citations.

claim: The natverse includes interactive functions, such as nlscan, that allow users to visually scan neurons and identify mis-assignments.
source: The natverse includes interactive functions, such as nlscan, that allow users to visually scan neurons and identify mis-assignments (Figure 4c), or find.neuron and find.soma, that allow users to select a neuron of interest from a 3D window (Figure 4c).
evidence: Stated as a capability with reference to a figure.

claim: In smaller brains, like insect central brains or larval fish central brains, the overlap of both axons and dendrites in 3D space is an excellent starting point for defining a neuronal type.
source: In smaller brains, like insect central brains or larval fish central brains, the overlap of both axons and dendrites in 3D space is an excellent starting point for defining a neuronal type, since neurite apposition is suggestive of synaptic connectivity (Rees et al., 2017) and neurites are highly stereotyped (Jenett et al., 2012; Pascual et al., 2004).
evidence: Stated with citations.

claim: It is highly desirable to compare neurons between datasets within a singular template space.
source: It is highly desirable to compare neurons between datasets within a singular template space.
evidence: Stated as a motivation for the work.

claim: Separate template brains 'contain' many large and useful but disparate datasets for D. melanogaster.
source: Considering just the case of D. melanogaster, separate template brains 'contain' many large and useful but disparate datasets (Table 1):~23,000 single light-level neuronal morphologies, hundreds of neuronal tracings from dye fills, a collection of ~11,000 genetic driver lines, ~100 neuroblast clones, and connectomic data, including a brainwide draft connectome on the horizon (Scheffer and Meinertzhagen, 2019; Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated with reference to a table and citations.

claim: Two approaches have been taken in specifying template spaces: choosing a single brain or creating an average brain.
source: Two approaches have been taken in specifying template spaces: a) choosing a single brain avoids any potential artifacts generated by the averaging procedure, but b) an average brain can reduce the impact of biological variation across individuals and deformations introduced during sample preparation, thus increasing the likelihood of successful and accurate registration (Bogovic et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated with citation.

claim: Quantitative neuroanatomical work requires images to be spatially calibrated.
source: Quantitative neuroanatomical work requires images to be spatially calibrated (i.e. with an accurate voxel size), but such calibrations are not present in all template brains.
evidence: Stated as a requirement.

claim: A simple 180° flip about the medio-lateral axis is insufficient to generate a left-right mirror for most neuroanatomical volumes.
source: Whilst the Drosophila brain is highly symmetric it is not perfectly so and the physical handling of brains during sample preparation introduces further non-biological asymmetries. A simple 180° flip about the medio-lateral axis is therefore insufficient (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Stated with reference to a figure.

claim: Non-rigid warping registrations have been constructed for a number of template spaces that introduce the small displacements required to fix the mapping from one hemisphere to the other.
source: To counter this, we have constructed non-rigid warping registrations for a number of template spaces that introduce the small displacements required to fix the mapping from one hemisphere to the other (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, see Materials and methods).
evidence: Stated as work done with reference to a figure.

claim: The mirroring procedure does not introduce any systematic errors into neuron morphology.
source: Our mirroring procedure (see Materials and methods) does not introduce any systematic errors into neuron morphology.
evidence: Stated as a property of the mirroring procedure.

claim: The distributions of NBLAST similarity scores between DL2d projection neurons from the same side of the brain and from alternate sides of the brain are not significantly different.
source: We do not find the distributions of scores (Figure 5c) to be significantly different (D = 0.025, p=0.094, two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test).
evidence: Stated as a statistical result with reference to a figure.

claim: The distribution of scores suggest that most bilateral neurons are reasonably symmetric.
source: Interestingly, the distribution of scores suggest that most bilateral neurons are reasonably symmetric.
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data.

claim: Simply rescaling a sample image to match a reference brain usually fails due to differences in position and rotation.
source: Simply rescaling a sample image to match a reference brain usually fails due to differences in position and rotation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Stated with reference to a figure.

claim: An affine transformation can account for differences in position and rotation, but not for differences in shape that may be of biological or experimental origin.
source: An affine transformation can account for these differences, but not for differences in shape that may be of biological or experimental origin.
evidence: Stated as a limitation of affine transformations.

claim: A full non-rigid warping deformation is used to correct for differences in shape.
source: To correct for these, we use a full non-rigid warping deformation, as described previously (Jefferis et al., 2007; Rohlfing and Maurer, 2003; Rueckert et al., 1999), see our Materials and methods.
evidence: Stated with citations.

claim: The use of a mutual information metric based on image intensity avoids the requirement for landmarks to be added to each image.
source: The use of a mutual information metric based on image intensity avoids the requirement for landmarks to be added to each image – a time-consuming task that can often introduce significant inaccuracies.
evidence: Stated as an advantage of the approach.

claim: The approach allows for the unsupervised registration of images and the independent nature of each registration allows the process to be parallelised across CPU cores.
source: Our approach allows for the unsupervised registration of images and the independent nature of each registration allows the process to be parallelised across CPU cores.
evidence: Stated as advantages of the approach.

claim: By utilizing a high-performance computational cluster, the entire FlyCircuit dataset was re-registered with high accuracy within a day.
source: By utilizing a high-performance computational cluster, we re-registered, with high accuracy, the entire FlyCircuit dataset within a day.
evidence: Stated as an achievement.

claim: The creation of a bridge between a GAL4 expression library and images of single neurons facilitates the decomposition of an expression pattern into its constituent neurons.
source: The creation of a bridge between a GAL4 expression library, such as the GMR collection (Jenett et al., 2012), and images of single neurons, such as those of FlyCircuit (Chiang et al., 2011), facilitates the decomposition of an expression pattern into its constituent neurons, allowing the correct assessment of innervation density on, for example, ipsilateral and contralateral sides (Figure 6—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: Stated with citations and reference to a figure.

claim: Correspondences between neuroblast clones can be identified with co-visualisation.
source: Similarly, correspondences between neuroblast clones can be identified with co-visualisation.
evidence: Stated as a capability.

claim: The ability to bridge segmentations from one space to another is useful for checking innervation across datasets.
source: The ability to bridge segmentations from one space to another is useful for checking innervation across datasets.
evidence: Stated as a use case.

claim: Both the FlyLight and Vienna Tiles libraries contain a wealth of GAL4 lines amenable to intersectional strategies.
source: Both the FlyLight (Jenett et al., 2012) and Vienna Tiles libraries (Tirian and Dickson, 2017) contain a wealth of GAL4 lines amenable to intersectional strategies (Luan et al., 2006).
evidence: Stated with citations.

claim: As the two libraries are registered to different template spaces, it is difficult to predict which combinations of a FlyLight GMR line with a Vienna Tiles line would produce a good intersection from the raw images provided by both.
source: However, as the two libraries are registered to different template spaces, it is difficult to predict which combinations of a FlyLight GMR line with a Vienna Tiles line would produce a good intersection (split-GAL4, targeting one cell type present in both parent lines) from the raw images provided by both.
evidence: Stated as a problem.

claim: Bridging one library into the space of another enables direct co-visualisation.
source: Bridging one library into the space of another (Figure 6—figure supplement 2i) enables direct co-visualisation (see also Otsuna et al. (2018) for an independent bridging output).
evidence: Stated with reference to a figure and citation.

claim: It is possible to warp 3D neuropils and neuron skeletons onto some target, without using landmark pairs, using Deformetrica.
source: It is also possible to warp 3D neuropils and neuron skeletons onto some target, without using landmark pairs. For this, Deformetrica (Bône et al., 2018; Durrleman et al., 2014) can be used to compute many pairwise registrations at once for different kinds of 3D objects to produce a single deformation of ambient 3D space describing a registration (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Stated with citations and reference to a figure.

claim: Finding neurons of the same cell type between a high-resolution EM dataset and light-level images of neurons is an essential step in identifying neurons and their genetic resources.
source: Finding neurons of the same cell type between a high-resolution EM dataset and light-level images of neurons (Figure 7a) is an essential step in identifying neurons and their genetic resources.
evidence: Stated with reference to a figure.

claim: Linking EM and LM data connects connectivity and detailed morphology information acquired at the nanometer resolution to other forms of data.
source: So doing links connectivity and detailed morphology information acquired at the nanometer resolution to other forms of data.
evidence: Stated as a benefit.

claim: Linking EM and LM data can most easily be done by finding corresponding landmarks in EM data and a LM template space to build a registration.
source: This can most easily be done by finding corresponding landmarks in EM data and a LM template space to build a registration (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated with reference to a figure.

claim: The R package elmr can be used to select an anatomical locus from 3D plotted light-level neurons and generate a URL that specifies its correct coordinates in a FAFB14 CATMAID instance.
source: The R package elmr can be used to select an anatomical locus, here the PD2 primary neurite tract (Frechter et al., 2019), from 3D plotted light-level neurons, taken from FlyCircuit, and generate a URL that specifies its correct coordinates in a FAFB14 CATMAID instance.
evidence: Stated as a capability with citation.

claim: Close matches between EM and LM data reveal likely morphology of non-reconstructed branches but also contain off-target expression.
source: Close matches reveal likely morphology of non-reconstructed branches (orange arrow) but also contain off-target expression (yellow arrow).
evidence: Stated as an observation.

claim: Because close light-level matches for in-progress EM reconstructions reveal the likely morphology of non-reconstructed branches, this process can help human annotators reconstruct neurons accurately and in a targeted manner.
source: Further, because close light-level matches for in-progress EM reconstructions reveal the likely morphology of non-reconstructed branches (Figure 7c) this process can help human annotators reconstruct neurons accurately and in a targeted manner, which may be desirable given how time intensive the task is.
evidence: Stated with reference to a figure.

claim: The natverse was combined with a recent automatic segmentation of neurites in FAFB14 using a flood filling approach.
source: In order to further reduce this burden, we combined the natverse with a recent automatic segmentation of neurites in FAFB14 using a flood filling approach (Li et al., 2019), which produces volumetric fragments of neurites, where segments may be fairly large, ~100 μm in cable length.
evidence: Stated with citation.

claim: The fafbseg package includes functions to implement improved up-/downstream sampling of neurons based on automatic segmentation.
source: Our fafbseg package includes functions to implement improved up-/downstream sampling of neurons based on these segments, which we have recently discussed elsewhere (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated with citation.

claim: Volumetric reconstructions of manually traced neurons can be generated by mapping them onto volumetric data.
source: We can also generate volumetric reconstructions of manually traced neurons by mapping them onto volumetric data (Figure 8—figure supplement 1b), hosted by a brainmaps server and visible through a Neuroglancer instance (Figure 8—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Stated with reference to figures.

claim: Currently, ~500 automatic segments will map onto one accurately manually traced neuron but only ~20 segments may constitute the highest Strahler order branches.
source: Currently, ~500 such segments will map onto one accurately manually traced neuron but only ~20 segments may constitute the highest Strahler order branches meaning that manual concatenation of these fragments speeds up discovery of coarse morphologies by ~10 x (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated with citation.

claim: Twigs and small-calibre, lower Strahler order branches are more difficult to automatically segment.
source: Twigs and small-calibre, lower Strahler order branches are more difficult to automatically segment (Figure 8—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Stated with reference to a figure.

claim: A densely reconstructed connectome, with ~35% of synapses connected up for just under half of the central fly brain has recently been made available by the FlyEM team at Janelia Research Campus.
source: A densely reconstructed connectome, with ~35% of synapses connected up for just under half of the central fly brain has recently been made available by the FlyEM team at Janelia Research Campus (Scheffer and Meinertzhagen, 2019; Shan Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: Stated with citations.

claim: Neurons from the 'hemibrain' volume can be transformed to the JRC2018F light level template brain via a bridging registration.
source: Neurons from this 'hemibrain' volume can be transformed to the JRC2018F light level template brain via a bridging registration constructed using the strategy described by Bogovic et al. (2018).
evidence: Stated with citation.

claim: The bridging registration for the hemibrain has been wrapped within the natverse framework.
source: We have already wrapped this bridging registration within the natverse framework, thereby connecting it to the full network of fly template brains, datasets and analysis tools already described in this paper.
evidence: Stated as work done.

claim: The shape of a neuron is of major functional significance.
source: The shape of a neuron is of major functional significance.
evidence: Stated as background knowledge.

claim: Morphology is driven by and constrains connectivity.
source: Morphology is driven by and constrains connectivity.
evidence: Stated as background knowledge.

claim: Morphology is the primary means by which neuroscientists have historically identified neuron classes.
source: It is also the primary means by which neuroscientists have historically identified neuron classes.
evidence: Stated as background knowledge.

claim: There have been three main drivers behind the recent emphasis on quantitative neuroanatomy: the ever increasing scale of new approaches for acquiring image data and reconstructing neurons, a drive to formalise descriptions of the spatial properties of neurons and networks at various scales, and a desire to intuit the organisational principles behind different nervous tissues and correlate these findings with dynamic data on neuron activity.
source: There have been three main drivers behind the recent emphasis on quantitative neuroanatomy: a) the ever increasing scale of new approaches for acquiring image data and reconstructing neurons, b) a drive to formalise descriptions of the spatial properties of neurons and networks at various scales, and c) a desire to intuit the organisational principles behind different nervous tissues and correlate these findings with dynamic data on neuron activity.
evidence: Stated as context for the work.

claim: The natverse allows a user to read data from local or remote sources into R, and leverage both natverse functions and the >10,000 R packages on CRAN to aid their data analysis.
source: The natverse allows a user to read data from local or remote sources into R, and leverage both natverse functions and the >10,000 R packages on CRAN (and more on Bioconductor, Neuroconductor, GitHub, etc.) to aid their data analysis.
evidence: Stated as a capability.

claim: Users may call natverse R functions from other languages such as Python, Julia, MATLAB.
source: Users may also call natverse R functions from other languages such as Python, Julia, MATLAB.
evidence: Stated as a capability.

claim: The natverse is an actively developing project.
source: We note that the natverse is an actively developing project and also anticipate a) an increasing interest in dealing with neurons as volumes as automatic segmentation of datasets becomes commonplace, b) expanding our bridging tools to support a wider range of species, and to map between similar species and developmental stages, c) writing libraries to facilitate the use of the natverse in other programming languages and toolboxes besides Python, and d) expanding the range of neurogeometric analysis algorithms readily available in the natverse.
evidence: Stated as future directions.

claim: High-quality bridging registrations have been created between new template spaces and brains in the hub.
source: High-quality bridging registrations would be created between new template spaces and brains in the hub, ensuring that any template could be bridged to any other via appropriate concatenations and inversions of these registrations.
evidence: Stated as work done.

claim: Using these resources, it is now possible to co-visualise and analyse more than 23,000 single neuron images, expression patterns of >9500 GAL4 lines and a near complete set of ~100 adult neuroblast clone lineage data.
source: Using these resources, it is now possible to co-visualise and analyse more than 23,000 single neuron images (Chiang et al., 2011), expression patterns of >9500 GAL4 lines (Jenett et al., 2012; Kvon et al., 2014; Tirian and Dickson, 2017) and a near complete set of ~100 adult neuroblast clone lineage data (Ito et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2013) and easily combine these data with the standard insect brain name nomenclature system (Ito et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated with citations.

claim: It will soon be possible to identify split-GAL4 lines, a synaptic EM reconstruction and the developmental clone of origin for any given neuron or neuronal cell type for D. melanogaster.
source: It will soon be possible to identify split-GAL4 lines, a synaptic EM reconstruction and the developmental clone of origin for any given neuron or neuronal cell type for D. melanogaster.
evidence: Stated as an anticipated capability.

claim: If an experimenter is able to register their functional imaging data to a template brain space, they may be able to directly link it to cell types discovered in other datasets, including EM datasets.
source: Significantly, if an experimenter is able to register their functional imaging data to a template brain space (Mann et al., 2017; Pacheco et al., 2019), or alternatively identify neuroanatomical features in that data that can be used to build a landmark-based affine or thin-plate spline registration (e.g. using Morpho Schlager, 2017), they may be able to directly link it to cell types discovered in other datasets, including EM datasets.
evidence: Stated with citations.

claim: The near future will see generation of EM data for multiple whole adult Dipteran brains and larval zebrafish, possibly from different sexes and species.
source: The near future will see generation of EM data for multiple whole adult Dipteran brains and larval zebrafish, possibly from different sexes and species, as well as quality automatic segmentations for such data's neurites (Funke et al., 2019; Januszewski et al., 2018) and synapses (Heinrich et al., 2018), even from anisotropic serial section transmission EM data (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated with citations.

claim: Interpreting high-resolution EM connectomic data will be accelerated and enriched by making links to light level data.
source: Interpreting high-resolution EM connectomic data will be accelerated and enriched by making links to light level data (Schlegel et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated with citation.

claim: It is possible that connectomes and transcriptomes may be linked on a cell type basis, using neuron morphology as a bridge.
source: Furthermore, it is possible that connectomes and transcriptomes may be linked on a cell type basis, using neuron morphology as a bridge (Bates et al., 2019).
evidence: Stated with citation.

claim: The natverse provides extensible functionality for easily combining and analysing all these data.
source: The natverse provides extensible functionality for easily combining and analysing all these data.

claim: The catmaid package provides application programming interface (API) access to the CATMAID web image annotation tool.
source: The package catmaid provides application programming interface (API) access to the CATMAID web image annotation tool (Saalfeld et al., 2009; Schneider-Mizell et al., 2016).

claim: CATMAID is a common choice for communities using terabyte-scale EM data to manually reconstruct neuron morphologies and annotate synaptic locations.
source: CATMAID is a common choice for communities using terabyte-scale EM data to manually reconstruct neuron morphologies and annotate synaptic locations (Berck et al., 2016; Dolan et al., 2018a; Eichler et al., 2017; Frechter et al., 2019; Ohyama et al., 2015; Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated with citations.

claim: Users can use catmaid to read CATMAID neurons into R including the locations and associations of their synapses, and other tags that might identify biological entities such as somata, microtubules or gap junctions.
source: Users can use catmaid to read CATMAID neurons into R including the locations and associations of their synapses, and other tags that might identify biological entities such as somata, microtubules or gap junctions.
evidence: Stated as a capability.

claim: Users can leverage CATMAID's infrastructure of flexible hierarchical semantic annotations to make queries for neurons for example in a brain region of interest.
source: Users can also leverage CATMAID's infrastructure of flexible hierarchical semantic annotations to make queries for neurons for example in a brain region of interest.
evidence: Stated as a capability.

claim: catmaid can edit CATMAID databases directly, for example by adding annotations, uploading neurons, synapses and meshes.

evidence: Stated as a capability.

claim: catmaid can enable a user to send authenticated requests to a CATMAID server, so data can be kept private but still be read into R over an Internet connection.
source: In this case, catmaid can enable a user to send authenticated requests to a CATMAID server, that is data can be kept private but still be read into R over an Internet connection.
evidence: Stated as a capability.

claim: neuromorphr provides an R client for the NeuroMorpho.org API.
source: neuromorphr provides an R client for the NeuroMorpho.org API (Ascoli et al., 2007; Halavi et al., 2008; Nanda et al., 2015), a curated inventory of reconstructed neurons (n = 107395, 60 different species) that is updated as new reconstructions are collected and published.
evidence: Stated with citations.

claim: NeuroMorpho.org is a curated inventory of reconstructed neurons (n = 107395, 60 different species) that is updated as new reconstructions are collected and published.
source: neuromorphr provides an R client for the NeuroMorpho.org API (Ascoli et al., 2007; Halavi et al., 2008; Nanda et al., 2015), a curated inventory of reconstructed neurons (n = 107395, 60 different species) that is updated as new reconstructions are collected and published.
evidence: Stated with citations.

claim: insectbrainr can retrieve neurons and brain region surface models from InsectBrainDB.org (n = 139 neurons, 14 species).
source: insectbrainr can retrieve neurons and brain region surface models from InsectBrainDB.org (n = 139 neurons, 14 species).
evidence: Stated as a capability.

claim: flycircuit interacts with the flycircuit.tw project, which contains >23,000 registered and skeletonised D. melanogaster neurons.
source: Similarly flycircuit interacts with the flycircuit.tw project (Chiang et al., 2011; Shih et al., 2015), which contains >23,000 registered and skeletonised D. melanogaster neurons.
evidence: Stated with citations.

claim: The vfbr package can pull image data from VirtualFlyBrain.org, which hosts registered stacks of central nervous system image data for D. melanogaster.
source: The vfbr package can pull image data from VirtualFlyBrain.org, which hosts registered stacks of central nervous system image data for D. melanogaster, including image stacks for the major GAL4 genetic driver line collections (Jenett et al., 2012), neuroblast clones (Ito et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2013) and FlyCircuit's stochastically labelled neurons (Chiang et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated with citations.

claim: The fishatlas package interacts with FishAtlas.neuro.mpg.de, which contains 1709 registered neurons from the larval Danio rerio.
source: The fishatlas package interacts with FishAtlas.neuro.mpg.de, which contains 1709 registered neurons from the larval Danio rerio (Kunst et al., 2019), while mouselightr does the same for the MouseLight project at Janelia Research Campus (Economo et al., 2016), which has generated >1000 morphologies.
evidence: Stated with citations.

claim: The MouseLight project at Janelia Research Campus has generated >1000 morphologies.
source: The fishatlas package interacts with FishAtlas.neuro.mpg.de, which contains 1709 registered neurons from the larval Danio rerio (Kunst et al., 2019), while mouselightr does the same for the MouseLight project at Janelia Research Campus (Economo et al., 2016), which has generated >1000 morphologies.
evidence: Stated with citations.

source: The package nat.ants wraps the R package ANTsRCore (Kandel et al., 2019) with a small number of functions to enable nat functions to use Advanced Normalisation Tools (ANTs) registrations (Avants et al., 2009).

claim: The R package deformetricar does the same for the non-image based registration software Deformetrica without the need for landmark correspondences.
source: The R package deformetricar does the same for the non-image (e.g. mesh or line data) based registration software Deformetrica (Bône et al., 2018; Durrleman et al., 2014) without the need for landmark correspondences.

source: The nat package already contains functions to support CMTK registrations (Rohlfing and Maurer, 2003).
evidence: Stated with citation.

source: The nat.templatebrains package extends nat to explicitly include the notion of each neuron belonging to a certain template space, as well as functions to deploy bridging and mirroring registrations.
evidence: Stated as a capability.

claim: nat.flybrains contains mesh data describing commonly used template spaces for D. melanogaster as well as CMTK bridging and mirror deformations.
source: Additionally, nat.flybrains contains mesh data describing commonly used template spaces for D. melanogaster as well as CMTK bridging and mirror deformations discussed in the latter half of the results section.

claim: nat.nblast allows users to deploy the NBLAST neuron similarity algorithm by pairwise comparison of vector clouds describing these neurons in R.
source: nat.nblast allows users to deploy the NBLAST neuron similarity algorithm (Costa et al., 2016), by pairwise comparison of vector clouds describing these neurons in R.

claim: The nabor package is a wrapper for libnabo, a k-nearest neighbour library which is optimised for low dimensional (e.g. 3D) spaces.

claim: The package elmr allows users to read neurons from the FAFB CATMAID environment, transform them into a template space where they can be compared with light-level neurons, then visualised and/or NBLAST-ed.
source: The package elmr allows users to read neurons from this environment, transform them into a template space where they can be compared with light-level neurons for which the community may have some other information (e.g. gene expression, functional characterisation, presence in genetic drive lines, etc.), then visualised and/or NBLAST-ed; all with only a few lines of code.
evidence: Stated as a capability.

claim: elmr enables CATMAID users to perform interim analyses as they reconstruct neurons, helping them to choose interesting targets for reconstruction and identify manually traced or automatically reconstructed neuron fragments or anatomical landmarks such as fiber tracts.
source: This process enables CATMAID users to perform interim analyses as they reconstruct neurons, helping them to choose interesting targets for reconstruction and identify manually traced or automatically reconstructed neuron fragments (Dolan et al., 2019) or anatomical landmarks such as fiber tracts (Frechter et al., 2019), and so improve the efficiency of their targeted circuit reconstructions (Dolan et al., 2018a; Felsenberg et al., 2018; Huoviala et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated with citations.

claim: Full, non-rigid warping registrations were computed using the Computational Morphometry Toolkit (CMTK), as described previously.
source: Full, non-rigid warping registrations were computed using the Computational Morphometry Toolkit (CMTK), as described previously (Jefferis et al., 2007).
evidence: Stated with citation.

claim: An initial rigid affine registration with twelve degrees of freedom (translation, rotation and scaling of each axis) was followed by a non-rigid registration that allows different brain regions to move somewhat independently, subject to a smoothness penalty.
source: An initial rigid affine registration with twelve degrees of freedom (translation, rotation and scaling of each axis) was followed by a non-rigid registration that allows different brain regions to move somewhat independently, subject to a smoothness penalty (Rueckert et al., 1999).
evidence: Stated with citation.

claim: In the non-rigid step, deformations between the independently moving control points are interpolated using B-splines, with image similarity being computed through the use of a normalised mutual information metric.
source: In the non-rigid step, deformations between the independently moving control points are interpolated using B-splines, with image similarity being computed through the use of a normalised mutual information metric (Studholme et al., 1999).
evidence: Stated with citation.
